text.p: Australian inventories (stocks) rose by 1.2 percent in the December quarter, official figures on Monday showed.
Economists' forecasts had centred on a 1.2 percent rise.

Also released was the first monthly balance of international trade on goods and services, which has taken the place of the monthly balance of payments. The figure was a deficit of A$63 million for January.
Forecasts centred on a median deficit of A$230 million.
A selection of economists' immediate reactions to the data follow:
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"I'd like to see the revisions for the September quarter before I stuck my neck out and had an estimate on what it means for December quarter GDP, but if we've had a downward revision to the inventory accumulation for the September quarter clearly that means that the September quarter GDP growth rate will be revised down and...earlier fears about a very weak December quarter GDP number are not quite as severe as they appeared at first."
HANS KUNNEN, CHIEF ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK:

"I don't think it's going to change our overall GDP outlook by that much at this stage. We're actually looking for a fairly weak rise in GDP, and the stocks are going to give a small negative to that figure.(On the goods and services balance) It's pleasing to see it lower than expectations, imports and exports are roughly in balance. The problem area remains debt and servicing that debt, so it's encouraging our trade position isn't really bad, and I think that should be supportive of the currency."
RIC SIMES, CHIEF ECONOMIST, ROTHSCHILD AUSTRALIA:

"On the trade side...it appears to us that the overall balance would be consistent with a current account deficit of the order of A$1.6 billion or so. That's running at a moderate level. It's not unduly high at a time when the economy is reasonably soft and so we can expect that to widen as the year progresses. On stocks, the big change is the revisions to the September quarter numbers and as a result of those, we saw stocks continue to build up in the December quarter but at a similar pace to September. What does that mean for the economy? Not all that much. We still would expect some correction to stocks over the next few quarters and that will tend to put a bit of a dampener on growth
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST MACQUARIE BANK:

"The much talked about stock run-up now looks much smaller. It looks like stocks are more in line with firm sales. Hence you wouldn't be expecting as big a run-down in stocks and you clearly haven't seen that in the December quarter. As a consequence, stocks will not be subtracting very much at all in the December quarter. And I would imagine that mechanically it's going to push up people's forecasts for the expenditure component of GDP by perhaps around 0.3 percentage points."
ROB HENDERSON, CHIEF ECONOMIST, DRESDNER AUSTRALIA:

"The outcome for stocks is pretty much in line with our expectations. Basically, it's sort of neutral for GDP forecasts, so we're not revising our forecasts on the back of these numbers. I guess the real surprise was the goods and services balance, where to us the number's considerably better than we had expected, but also it's far better than the market was expecting. The export performance overall was far better than expected. The clear implication of this is that it's slightly positive for the Aussie dollar. Obviously, it will tend to allay concerns of the current account blowing out during 1997."
MATTHEW DRENNAN, ECONOMIST, AXIOM FUNDS MANAGEMENT:

"(The trade balance was) a bit lower than expected. I still think the trend in terms of the current account deficit is going to be a deteriorating one over 1997, but it's just in neutral territory at the moment, it's not something the markets are really worrying about. One of the interesting points was that the export side seems to have held up very, very well in the month...so that's encouraging. (On stocks) I think it puts the risks to GDP on the upside, because while the quarterly increase was in line, we're working from a lower base there (due to the revisions)."
